 Sharp ratio. Explained with a worm. This separates amateur investors from billionaires. Here are two investments. Both made 40%. Which one is better? By return alone, you can't say. So look at the path each one took. The first climbed steadily. The second wiggles all over the place with one steep drop in the middle. Those wiggles are bad for three reasons. One, they're painful to hold. One month you're ahead. The next you're way down with no idea if you'll get back. Two, you can't trust it. After wiggling that much, it could do anything next. Three, you might need the cash. Need it on a down day and you sell it a loss. Those wiggles have a proper name. Risk. So the second investment is worse. It took far more risk to earn the same return. Returns can't see that. We need a number that can. First, put a number on the wiggles. Draw the trend line. Measure how far the investment strays from it. That's volatility. Then divide. Average return divided by volatility. That's the sharp ratio. How much return you earn for each unit of risk you take. More return, it goes up. More wiggles, it goes down. The steady one scores two. The wild one, one half. What does that feel like? At one half, you lose money roughly one year in three. At two, roughly one year in 40. At 20, the wiggles are gone. A straight line, up and to the right. You would almost never see a losing month. Impossible. One high-speed trading firm reported a single losing day in nearly five years. That's why this is the number one metric for quants. Fewer wiggles means more proof it's skill, not luck. And it shows you what to mix. Take two investments, each scoring two. When one zigs, the other zags. Hold both and the wiggles cancel. The score jumps to five. But you can't eat a sharp ratio. What if the smooth one earns less? Then you borrow. Borrow a dollar for each dollar you have and the return doubles. So do the wiggles. The score stays the same. So a smooth investment with borrowed money can beat a wild one and still be smoother. Careful. Borrow too much and you can blow up. So yes, returns matter. But so does risk. Don't just ask how much it made. Ask how much it wiggled. Aside from the sharp ratio, there's one more number you must master in investing. Comment your guess. Then follow to find out.
